name: ADUM1250ARZ-RL7
title: ADuM1250 / ADuM1251: hot-swappable dual I2C digital isolators, 2500 V rms, SOIC-8
summary: Two-channel digital isolators for I2C, SMBus and PMBus lines, built on on-chip transformer (iCoupler) coupling. Each open-drain bus pin stays a single bidirectional wire on both sides, so no separate transmit and receive paths are needed. The ADuM1250 carries both SDA and SCL in both directions; the ADuM1251 carries SDA in both directions and SCL from Side 1 to Side 2 only. Each side runs from 3.0 V to 5.5 V up to 1000 kHz, Side 2 sinks up to 30 mA, and hot-swap circuitry keeps the bus quiet while a card is plugged in unpowered. The barrier is rated 2500 V rms for one minute.

circuits.title: Typical isolated I2C interface (ADuM1250)
circuits.description: An ADuM1250 joins a local I2C bus on Side 1 to an isolated I2C bus on Side 2. Each bus line has its own pull-up to its own side's supply: R1 and R2 pull SDA1 and SCL1 to VDD1, R3 and R4 pull SDA2 and SCL2 to VDD2. C1 and C2, 0.01 µF to 0.1 µF, bypass each supply pin to its own ground. R5, 200 Ω in series between VDD1 and pin 1, is required for latch-up immunity where the ambient can lie between 105 °C and 125 °C; the Side 1 pull-ups take VDD1 ahead of it.

parts.note: optional; needed for latch-up immunity above 105 °C ambient

notes: Without R5, VDD1 runs straight to pin 1.

operation.text: Inside, each bidirectional bus pin pair is two one-way channels pointed opposite ways, each crossing the barrier on its own iCoupler transformer. One senses the Side 1 pin and drives the Side 2 pin; the other does the reverse. A low on either pin pulls the opposite pin low enough for other I2C devices to read it as a low. In the ADuM1251 the clock has only the Side 1 to Side 2 channel.

Side 1 is kept from latching the bus by its input threshold, which is at least 50 mV below its own output low level. A low that Side 1 drives because Side 2 is low is therefore not read back as a Side 1 input and sent back across.

Side 2 uses standard I2C thresholds (input low at 0.3 VDD2) and is I2C-compliant, so several isolators can share one bus on their Side 2 pins together with other I2C devices. Side 1 has a shifted output low and input threshold and is I2C-compatible only: it talks with devices that meet the I2C standard. The output low levels do not depend on VDD1 or VDD2, and the Side 1 input threshold does not depend on VDD1. Both sides have open-collector outputs pulled high by resistors to their own supply, for buses from 3.0 V to 5.5 V.

Each supply has an undervoltage lockout. The channels start only once both supplies are at or above 2.5 V and 40 µs have passed since both crossed the internal 2.0 V start-up threshold. Until then the outputs on both sides stay high, so power-up and power-down put no lows on the bus. Recommended operation starts at 3.0 V. The 40 µs delay applies at supply slew rates both above and below 12.5 V/ms.
Both parts carry hot-swap circuitry that keeps an unpowered card from glitching data when it is plugged into a live bus.

Each side needs a 0.01 µF to 0.1 µF capacitor from VDD1 to GND1 and from VDD2 to GND2. Where ambient temperature may lie between 105 °C and 125 °C, latch-up immunity calls for a 200 Ω resistor in series with VDD1.

The parts run to 1 Mbps. Side 1 has little sink current, so at 1 Mbps and the smallest pull-up it drives 40 pF at most. At 100 kbps standard mode and 400 kbps fast mode much more is allowed; a larger pull-up reduces the allowed capacitance in proportion.

Failure would need a field strong enough to induce a voltage in a receiving coil that falsely sets or resets the decoder; the 3 V condition is the most sensitive. Transformer output pulses exceed 1.0 V and the decoder threshold is near 0.5 V, leaving a 0.5 V margin. At 1 MHz the allowed field is 0.2 kgauss, which induces 0.25 V, about half the threshold; during a pulse of the worst polarity it would cut a >1.0 V pulse to 0.75 V. As a current, 0.5 kA at 1 MHz passing 5 mm from the part is needed to disturb it. Strong high-frequency fields can still induce errors in PCB trace loops feeding later circuits, so such loops are to be kept small in layout.
